phase1.intro:
The storage room is organized. Every program up to this point has still been one worker doing one thing at a time.

Where should we start?

topics.buttonText: What's the difference between a process and a thread?
dialogue: A running Java program is a [[term:process]] — its own chunk of memory, isolated from every other program. A [[term:thread]] is a worker inside that process. [[fun:Every program you've written so far has had exactly one thread — the main thread]].

stickyNote.flavor: 🏢 the building vs. the workers inside it
stickyNote.definition: A process is an isolated running program with its own memory. A thread is a worker inside that process — every program so far has had just one, the main thread.

topics.buttonText: What do multiple threads actually share?
dialogue: [[warn:The part that makes this genuinely new is what they share]]: every thread gets its own stack, but they all share the same heap — the same objects, the same collections. Two workers reaching into the same storage bin at the same instant is exactly the danger.

stickyNote.definition: Each thread has its own stack (local variables) but all threads share the same heap (objects, fields) — the source of concurrency danger.

topics.buttonText: Why bother with multithreading at all?
dialogue: [[key:Why bother, then?]] Parallelism — genuinely doing independent work at once on a multi-core CPU — and responsiveness — keeping the main thread free while a slow task runs elsewhere. [[warn:More threads is not automatically faster]] — coordinating between them has a real cost of its own.

stickyNote.flavor: ⚡ parallelism and responsiveness, not automatic speed
stickyNote.definition: Multithreading enables parallelism (true simultaneous work) and responsiveness (main thread stays free) — but more threads isn't automatically faster.

phase1.openingDialogue: Multithreading puts multiple workers in the same process, sharing the same heap — powerful, but genuinely riskier than one worker at a time. ⚡

phase2.explanation:
Conceptual lesson — no broken code!

Common misconception: "More threads always means better performance."

Actually: More threads can reduce performance due to:
• Context switching overhead
• Memory consumption
• Increased complexity
• Limited CPU cores

Recommendation: Number of threads ≈ Number of CPU cores (for CPU-bound tasks)

Another misconception: "Threads are completely independent and don't interact."

Actually: Threads share memory and resources. This is what causes race conditions and deadlocks!

Example of a race condition:
Two threads both increment a shared counter: counter++
Thread A reads counter (5), Thread B reads counter (5)
Both increment (6), both write (6) — Should be 7!

Always use synchronization when sharing data between threads!

phase3.openingDialogue: Multithreading — doing multiple things at once! 🧵

mcq.question:
Which statement about multithreading is TRUE?

A) Adding more threads always makes a program faster
B) Threads share memory and can access the same data
C) A process cannot have multiple threads
D) All threads run in parallel on all CPUs
E) Threads never interact with each other

Select the CORRECT statement.

phase5.trivia: The number of hardware threads actually available on a machine is Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() — but that number is a hint, not a hard cap. Java happily lets you create thousands of Thread objects on a 4-core machine; the OS scheduler just switches between them faster than any human could notice, which is exactly the illusion of "simultaneous" this lesson is getting at.
